wine.name: Sauvignon Blanc Ried Zieregg
wine.classification: Riedenwein of the DAC, and a Grosse STK Ried in the growers' own classification
wine.sites: The Zieregg, the steep, south facing slope above the winery at Berghausen, on coralline limestone from an ancient reef with blue calcareous marl in places; the border with Slovenia runs across the hill.
wine.making: Picked by hand and fermented spontaneously, with no yeast added. The wine then rests on its lees in large, neutral oak casks for around two years, longer in some vintages, before bottling, as the house's own sheets describe it.
wine.glass: Gooseberry, white peach and orange zest over white apple, a hint of mint and a flinty edge; taut and precise, with fine acidity and a long, salty lemon finish.
wine.ageing: Tight in its first years, it opens after four or five and keeps for well over a decade in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The protected origin of Styria's southern hills along the Slovenian border, in force since the 2018 vintage.
Ried marks a named single vineyard; the Zieregg is the slope above the winery at Berghausen.
Grosse STK Ried: the upper tier of the site ranking the STK growers' association sets for its members.

records.table: Tement's Sauvignon Blanc Ried Zieregg comes from a steep slope of coral limestone above the winery, right on the Slovenian border. Fermented with its own yeasts and kept long in large old casks, it is taut, flinty and saline, a Sauvignon to cellar.
records.story: The Tement family dates its estate at Berghausen, in the hills of the Südsteiermark, to 1959, when it began with a small holding of vines, and by the house's own account the Zieregg, the slope above the farm, is where its story starts. When the founder died suddenly in 1976, his son took over while the Zieregg was a small vineyard, and staked the estate on Sauvignon Blanc from the limestone of the region. In 1986 he was among the growers who formed the Steirische Klassik group, as the sources tell it, from which the STK, the Styrian Terroir and Klassik estates, later grew. The STK ranks its members' sites as Erste and Grosse STK Ried, and the Zieregg sits in the upper tier. The hill is older than the border across it: the line between Austria and the new Yugoslavia was drawn after the First World War, and the Slovenian half of the slope is called Ciringa. In the 2000s the family began to farm that side too, under the name Domaine Ciringa. From the 2018 vintage the Südsteiermark became a DAC, and the Zieregg carries Ried on its label as a single vineyard wine. For a sommelier it shows Styrian Sauvignon Blanc grown on limestone and given time: taut, smoky and built to age.

others.name: Sauvignon Blanc Ried Grassnitzberg
others.note: An Erste STK Ried Sauvignon Blanc from a limestone reef near the winery, a vineyard planted in the 1950s by the house's account.

others.name: Domaine Ciringa Fosilni Breg
others.note: Sauvignon Blanc from the Slovenian half of the Zieregg slope, under the family's Slovenian label.

others.name: Morillon Ried Zieregg
others.note: Chardonnay under its old Styrian name, from the same slope as the flagship.

traps: Morillon on a Tement label is Chardonnay under its old Styrian name, not a separate grape.
Domaine Ciringa's Fosilni Breg grows on the Slovenian half of the same hill, so it carries a Slovenian origin, Štajerska, never Südsteiermark DAC.

cards.front: Tement's Zieregg: on what rock does the slope grow, and in which DAC?
cards.back: Coralline limestone from an ancient reef, with calcareous marl in places; Südsteiermark DAC.

cards.front: What is Ciringa to the Tement family?
cards.back: The Slovenian name and half of the Zieregg slope, cut off by the border drawn after the First World War, farmed as Domaine Ciringa.

questions.q: A guest asks how Tement raises its Sauvignon Blanc Ried Zieregg. Which description fits?
opts: Wild ferment, then long on lees in large neutral casks
Cultured yeast and a few months in steel
Barrique ferment with weekly stirring of the lees
Whole bunches under carbon dioxide, then steel
questions.exp: The house ferments the Zieregg with no added yeast and keeps it on its lees in large, neutral oak casks for around two years; it is never a short, steel raised wine.

questions.q: What split the Zieregg slope, leaving part of it on the Slovenian side under the name Ciringa?
opts: The border drawn after the First World War
The Austrian wine scandal of 1985
Austria's entry into the European Union
The founding of the Südsteiermark DAC
questions.exp: The hill was one site until the border between Austria and the new Yugoslavia was drawn after the First World War; the DAC came only with the 2018 vintage.

sources.title: Tement: Ried Zieregg Sauvignon Blanc 2020, fact sheet
Falstaff: Tement 2019 Sauvignon Blanc Südsteiermark DAC Ried Zieregg GSTK

report: The founding year 1959 rests on the house's own labels, wein.plus and Falstaff; one source gives 1979 and another 1980 for the son's start, which is the takeover of 1976 told differently.
The founder's name and dates are not given in two sources, so he is described, not named; every living member of the family is left unnamed.
The barrel time differs by vintage in the house's sheets (24 months for 2019, 30 for 2020, 20 in a merchant's sheet), so the record says around two years.
The year the family began to farm the Slovenian side differs (2004, 2005, 2007, first vintage 2009), so the story says the 2000s.
A German magazine's tasting of 1991 that ranked the house's Sauvignon Blanc is left out: it is a judgement of rank.

The 1986 founding of the Steirische Klassik group rests on wein.plus's glossary and Lebendige Weine; that Tement was among its founders is in Lebendige Weine and a tourism page of Steiermark that names Tement and Sattlerhof as founding members of the STK, so the story hedges it.

wine.name: Sauvignon Blanc Ried Kranachberg
wine.classification: Riedenwein of the DAC, and a Grosse STK Ried in the growers' own classification
wine.sites: The Kranachberg, a high, cool ridge between Gamlitz and Leutschach at 400 to 500 metres, on calcareous quartz sands with mica, manganese and iron over limestone gravel.
wine.making: Picked by hand from vineyards the family farms biodynamically, by its own account, and fermented in stainless steel, latterly with the vineyard's own yeasts, by the house's sheets. The wine is then raised on its lees in steel for many months before bottling.
wine.glass: Gooseberry, yellow tropical fruit and orange zest over a nutty note, with white stone fruit in cooler years; tight, juicy and complex, with a savoury, salty finish.
wine.ageing: Open after two or three years, it gains depth over a decade and more in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a young bottle opens with air; a white wine glass with a generous bowl.

label.means: The protected origin of Styria's southern hills along the Slovenian border, in force since the 2018 vintage.
Ried marks a named single vineyard; the Kranachberg is the ridge between Gamlitz and Leutschach.
Grosse STK Ried: the upper tier of the site ranking the STK growers' association sets for its members.

records.table: Sattlerhof's Sauvignon Blanc Ried Kranachberg grows on a high, cool ridge above Gamlitz, on limestone and quartz sands. Raised in steel on its lees rather than in oak, it is taut and juicy, gooseberry and orange zest with a salty finish.
records.story: At the heart of the Sattlerhof in Gamlitz stands a farmhouse first recorded in 1886, which by the house's account already kept vines, animals and fields. In the 1960s, as the family tells it, the head of the farm began to make wine without residual sugar, chaptalisation or acidification, true to its origin, a stance that stirred controversy in a region used to softer wines. He also took over the Pfarrweingarten, the parish priest's vineyard in Gamlitz, and replanted it, and with the 1977 vintage its name appeared on the label. His son took over the farm, then small, at eighteen, and it was he who planted the Kranachberg, a cool ridge between Gamlitz and Leutschach, mostly with Sauvignon Blanc; Falstaff has tasted it as a Grosse STK site from the 1993 vintage. From 1990 the family added a restaurant and then rooms, and the Sattlerhof became an inn as well as a winery. It is a member of the STK, the Styrian Terroir and Klassik estates, whose growers rank their own sites, and from the 2018 vintage the Südsteiermark became a DAC. The house has since gone over to biodynamic farming, and the next generation works in its cellar and vineyards. To a sommelier the Kranachberg shows the high, cool side of the Südsteiermark.

others.name: Sauvignon Blanc Ried Alter Kranachberg
others.note: From the older vines of the Kranachberg on limestone gravel, spontaneously fermented and kept two years in steel, as the house gives it.

others.name: Sauvignon Blanc Ried Sernauberg
others.note: An Erste STK Ried Sauvignon Blanc from the Sernauberg in the Gamlitz hills.

others.name: Ried Pfarrweingarten
others.note: The parish priest's old vineyard, replanted by the family and first named on its label with the 1977 vintage.

traps: Ried Kranachberg and Ried Alter Kranachberg are two labels of the house: the second is drawn from the older vines of the slope.
Sattlerhof's Kranachberg is raised in steel, not oak, so its weight comes from the site and long lees contact rather than from barrels.

cards.front: Sattlerhof's Kranachberg: where is the ridge, and on what soils?
cards.back: Between Gamlitz and Leutschach at 400 to 500 metres, on calcareous quartz sands over limestone gravel.

cards.front: Which Sattlerhof vineyard was first named on a label with the 1977 vintage?
cards.back: The Pfarrweingarten, the parish priest's vineyard, taken over and replanted by the family.

questions.q: A guest expects oak in Sattlerhof's Sauvignon Blanc Ried Kranachberg. How is it raised?
opts: In stainless steel on its lees
In new French barriques
In clay amphorae with skin contact
In chestnut casks for five years
questions.exp: The house ferments and raises the Kranachberg in stainless steel on its lees, as its sheets and Falstaff record; there is no new oak.

questions.q: What did the head of the Sattlerhof do in the 1960s that stirred controversy, as the family tells it?
opts: Made wine with no residual sugar or chaptalisation
Planted Blauer Wildbacher for rosé
Sold the farm's wine only in bulk
Built a cellar for sparkling wine
questions.exp: He made wines true to their origin, without residual sugar, chaptalisation or acidification; Blauer Wildbacher is the Schilcher grape of the Weststeiermark, not of Gamlitz.

sources.title: Sattlerhof: Ried Kranachberg Sauvignon blanc 2018, fact sheet
Falstaff: Sattlerhof 2019 Sauvignon Blanc Südsteiermark DAC Ried Kranachberg GSTK
Regal Wine Co: Sattlerhof producer page

report: Recent vintages from 2022 appear in Falstaff and on the house's sheets as Ried Alter Kranachberg GSTK, while Ried Kranachberg GSTK is listed to 2020; whether Alter Kranachberg replaces the Kranachberg label or sits beside it I could not settle, so the record keeps the plan's name and lists Alter Kranachberg among the others. The checker may weigh a swap of the wine's name alone.

No founding year: the farmhouse is first recorded in 1886 by the house's account and a merchant says the family has made wine since the late 1880s, but a third account has the elder Sattler arriving from Lower Austria in the 1960s, so founded is empty and the story says only what the house says of the farmhouse.
The year the Kranachberg was planted is not given clearly by the house; Falstaff's listing of a 1993 Kranachberg G STK is the earliest vintage found, so the story ties nothing earlier to it.
The house's claim to have been the first in the region to make wines without residual sugar (1966 in its German chronicle) is told only as a stance that stirred controversy, by the family's account.
Farming: the house calls itself biodynamic and a merchant says organic, so the record says biodynamic by the house's own account.
The living heads of the family and their children are left unnamed.

records.place: Ratsch an der Weinstrasse, Südsteiermark DAC, Steiermark

wine.name: Sauvignon Blanc Ried Nussberg
wine.classification: Riedenwein of the DAC, and a Grosse STK Ried in the growers' own classification
wine.sites: The Nussberg above Ratsch, a very steep slope facing south south west; the Sauvignon Blanc grows on Opok, the local calcareous marl, while other parts of the hill hold calcareous sandstone and a patch of volcanic soil.
wine.making: After a short time on the skins the grapes are pressed gently and the juice fermented spontaneously in large, neutral oak casks. The wine then rests on its lees for well over a year, in some vintages several years, and is bottled late, as the house's own listings describe it.
wine.glass: Gooseberry, guava and candied orange zest over a smoky, stony note, with peach and mango in riper years; taut and closely knit, with elegant acidity and a long, lemony, salty finish.
wine.ageing: Released late and already open, it gains depth for a decade and more.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The protected origin of Styria's southern hills along the Slovenian border, in force since the 2018 vintage.
The house's slope above Ratsch; earlier vintages printed it as Ratscher Nussberg.
Grosse STK Ried: the upper tier of the site ranking the STK growers' association sets for its members.

records.table: Gross's Sauvignon Blanc Ried Nussberg comes from a steep slope of calcareous marl above Ratsch, bought by the family in 1986. Fermented with its own yeasts in large old casks and kept long on its lees, it is taut, smoky and salty.
records.story: The Gross family dates its winegrowing to 1907, when a forebear bought a vineyard on the Witscheiner Herrenberg. After the First World War the new border left that hill in Slovenia, yet it stayed in the family's hands. In the 1980s the next generation turned the estate towards quality wine, and in 1986 the family bought a vineyard and farmhouse on the Nussberg above Ratsch, a slope the house says has been known for its wine since the thirteenth century; the previous owner, as the family tells it, left a bottle of Nussberger from 1868 in the attic. The wine was labelled Ratscher Nussberg in its early vintages and Ried Nussberg later, ranked a Grosse STK Ried by the STK, the Styrian Terroir and Klassik estates, of which the house is a member. In 2006 two sons took on the estate, and in 2018 and 2019 the family divided its work, one branch keeping the estate at Ratsch and the other the Slovenian vineyards under the name Vino Gross. From the 2018 vintage the Südsteiermark became a DAC. The Nussberg shows the patient side of the region: a Sauvignon Blanc raised slowly in wood and released when it has settled, which is why a sommelier can pour it older than most Styrian whites.

others.name: Sauvignon Blanc Ried Sulz
others.note: An Erste STK Ried Sauvignon Blanc from the Sulz.

others.name: Weissburgunder Ried Nussberg Stauder
others.note: Pinot Blanc from the Stauder, a plateau of the Nussberg on reddish brown soil rich in iron and manganese.

others.name: Sauvignon Blanc Privat
others.note: A late released selection kept up to fifty four months in wood and steel, a tribute to the family's forebears, as the house tells it.

traps: The Nussberg of Ratsch in the Südsteiermark is not the Nussberg of Vienna, the hill of Wiener Gemischter Satz above the Danube.
Vino Gross is the Slovenian branch of the family, with its own vineyards across the border; the Nussberg wine comes from Weingut Gross at Ratsch.

cards.front: Gross's Nussberg: what soil does its Sauvignon Blanc grow on, and what is it called locally?
cards.back: Calcareous marl, known in Styria as Opok.

cards.front: In which year did the Gross family buy its vineyard and farmhouse on the Nussberg?
cards.back: In 1986, with a farmhouse that came with it.

questions.q: Which Nussberg gives Gross's Sauvignon Blanc Ried Nussberg?
opts: The slope above Ratsch in the Südsteiermark
The hill above the Danube in Vienna
A volcanic cone near Straden
A gneiss ridge above Stainz
questions.exp: Gross's Nussberg is the steep slope of calcareous marl above Ratsch; Vienna's Nussberg is a different hill, known for Wiener Gemischter Satz.

questions.q: What became of the Gross family's first vineyard, bought on the Witscheiner Herrenberg in 1907?
opts: It fell to Slovenia under the border drawn after 1918
It was sold to pay for the Nussberg
It was cleared for grain after 1945
It became the first Grosse STK Ried
questions.exp: The new border after the First World War put the Herrenberg in Slovenia, yet the family kept it; the Nussberg was bought in 1986 without any sale of it.

sources.title: Falstaff: Gross 2010 Sauvignon Blanc Ratscher Nussberg Grosse STK Lage
Falstaff: Gross 2022 Sauvignon Blanc Südsteiermark DAC Ried Nussberg GSTK
VieVinum 2022: Gross, Ried Nussberg Sauvignon Blanc 2017

report: The forebear of 1907 and the father who modernised the estate in the 1980s are not named: their dates were not found in two sources, and the father may be living.

The cellar regime differs by vintage: the VieVinum exhibitor listing gives a wild ferment in large neutral casks and one to two years on lees for the 2017, then years in steel, and Falstaff gives 41 months in a large cask for the 2022; the record says well over a year, in some vintages several.
The claim, from one source only, that the family farmed the Nussberg from about 1550 to the late nineteenth century is left out.
The thirteenth century renown of the Nussberg and the bottle of 1868 rest on the house alone and are hedged as its account.
The year the father took over (1984 in most accounts) and the generation count (fifth or sixth) disagree between sources and are left out.

wine.name: Sauvignon Blanc Ried Moarfeitl
wine.classification: Riedenwein of the DAC, and a Grosse STK Ried in the growers' own classification
wine.sites: The Moarfeitl above Straden, the family's first vineyard, by its account: steep slopes facing south and south west and a high, flat plateau, on calcareous sandy loam over Sarmatian gravel rather than volcanic rock; replanted in 1990.
wine.making: Picked by hand, the grapes rest on their skins for about a day and a half before pressing. The juice ferments with its own yeasts, and the wine is raised on its fine lees in large oak casks for some eighteen months before a late bottling, as the house describes it.
wine.glass: Yellow gooseberry, cassis and orange peel over rosemary and dried herbs, with a hint of peach; taut yet silky, complex and long, with a saline finish.
wine.ageing: Approachable on release, it builds for a decade and more in a good vintage.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The protected origin of Styria's south east, named for its old volcanoes, in force since the 2018 vintage.
Ried marks a named single vineyard; the Moarfeitl above Straden was the family's first.
Grosse STK Ried: the upper tier of the site ranking the STK growers' association sets for its members.
Certified organic, as the estate's vineyards have been since the 2013 vintage.

records.table: Neumeister's Sauvignon Blanc Ried Moarfeitl comes from the family's first vineyard above Straden in the Vulkanland, on limestone sediments rather than volcanic rock. Kept long on its lees in large oak, it is herbal, silky and saline.
records.story: By the house's account the Moarfeitl above Straden was the first vineyard the Neumeister family owned, in the 1930s. Around 1970 the family took on the Saziani estate nearby, which the province of Styria had run, and joined it to its own vines. In the 1980s a new generation took charge, and the estate grew with the Styrian wine boom that followed the wine scandal of 1985. The Moarfeitl was replanted in 1990. The next generation took over the cellar in 2009 and turned the estate to organic farming, and its vineyards have been certified since the 2013 vintage. The house is a member of the STK, the Styrian Terroir and Klassik estates, which rank the Moarfeitl and the Saziani as Grosse STK Ried and the Klausen and the Steintal as Erste STK Ried. From the 2018 vintage the Vulkanland Steiermark became a DAC, named for the old volcanoes of the south east, though much of the soil around Straden is limestone sediment, sandstone and gravel. The family also farms old Sauvignon Blanc vines on the Buchberg, planted in 1937 by its account. To a sommelier the Moarfeitl teaches that Vulkanland is a name of place, not always of rock.

others.name: Grauburgunder Ried Saziani
others.note: Pinot Gris from the Saziani, the estate's other Grosse STK Ried, the land the family took on around 1970.

others.name: Sauvignon Blanc Alte Reben
others.note: From old vines on the Buchberg and the Klausen, planted in 1937, 1951 and 1967 by the house's account.

others.name: Sauvignon Blanc Straden
others.note: The village wine, the Ortswein tier of the Vulkanland Steiermark DAC.

traps: Vulkanland Steiermark does not mean every vineyard is volcanic: the Moarfeitl grows on limestone sediments and gravel.
Ried Saziani is the house's Grauburgunder site, not its Sauvignon Blanc flagship; both sites carry the Grosse STK Ried tier.

cards.front: Neumeister's Moarfeitl: what soil lies under it, despite the name of its DAC?
cards.back: Calcareous sandy loam over Sarmatian gravel: limestone sediments rather than volcanic rock.

cards.front: Which Neumeister vineyard was the family's first, by its own account, in the 1930s?
cards.back: The Moarfeitl above Straden, replanted in 1990.

questions.q: How does Neumeister raise its Sauvignon Blanc Ried Moarfeitl, as the house describes it?
opts: Skin contact, a wild ferment, then large oak on lees
Quick pressing and a few months in steel
New barriques with weekly stirring for a year
Concrete eggs and bottling the next spring
questions.exp: The grapes rest about a day and a half on their skins, ferment with their own yeasts and spend some eighteen months on fine lees in large oak; nothing about it is quick or steel raised.

questions.q: Which estate near Straden did the Neumeister family take on around 1970, after the province of Styria had run it?
opts: Saziani
Moarfeitl
Zieregg
Kranachberg
questions.exp: The Saziani estate was taken on from the province around 1970; the Moarfeitl was already the family's own, its first vineyard since the 1930s.

sources.title: Neumeister: Ried Moarfeitl Sauvignon Blanc GSTK Bio
Neumeister: Alte Reben Sauvignon Blanc Straden
Falstaff: Neumeister 2021 Sauvignon Blanc Vulkanland Steiermark DAC Ried Moarfeitl GSTK

report: The Moarfeitl's soil is the house's own account (calcareous sandy loam on Sarmatian gravel), so the plan's caution holds: it is not volcanic, and the record says so in a trap.
The Saziani was taken on in 1971 by wein.plus and in 1970 by another source, so the record says around 1970; the man who took it on is not named, his dates unfound.
The year the second generation took charge differs (1981 in wein.plus, the mid 1980s in the house's podcast), so the story says the 1980s; the living members of the family are not named.
The founding year is empty: the house dates its first vineyard only to the 1930s.
Left out for want of a second source: the conversion to organic farming from 2008, the hillside cellar of 1998 and the restaurant of 1987.
The region record calls Neumeister the Vulkanland's reference and speaks of volcanic soil; the record does not repeat the judgement, and the Moarfeitl is limestone sediment.

records.place: Langegg, St. Stefan ob Stainz, Weststeiermark DAC, Steiermark

wine.name: Schilcher Ried Hochgrail
wine.classification: Riedenwein, the single vineyard tier of the Weststeiermark DAC
wine.grapes: Blauer Wildbacher alone, as the rules for Schilcher require.
wine.sites: The Hochgrail, steep parcels facing south at about 550 metres above St. Stefan ob Stainz, on lean brown earth over gneiss.
wine.making: Picked by hand, as the Weststeiermark DAC requires, and made as a rosé: the juice of the dark Blauer Wildbacher is taken off its skins early, so the wine keeps a pale pink to onion skin colour, and it is bottled dry and young.
wine.glass: Wild strawberry, raspberry and a hint of plum over a salty, stony note from the gneiss; light, dry and sharp, with bracing acidity.
wine.ageing: Made to drink young, within two or three years of the harvest, while its fruit and acidity are fresh.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a white wine glass.

label.means: A rosé of Blauer Wildbacher alone, grown in Styria; with a DAC, only the Weststeiermark may print it.
The protected origin of western Styria around Stainz and Deutschlandsberg, in force since the 2018 vintage.
Ried marks a named single vineyard; the Hochgrail is a high slope of gneiss above St. Stefan ob Stainz.

records.table: Langmann's Schilcher Ried Hochgrail is the Weststeiermark's rosé of Blauer Wildbacher, from high slopes of gneiss above St. Stefan ob Stainz. Pale, dry and sharp with acidity, it tastes of wild strawberry with a salty edge: pour it cold and young.
records.story: By the family's own account, its forebears planted their first vineyards at Langegg, above St. Stefan ob Stainz in the Weststeiermark, in 1746, with Blauer Wildbacher and a field blend. The farm is known by its old house name, vulgo Lex, which the family thinks comes from an earlier owner called Alexander, and some of its bottles read Lex Langmann. Blauer Wildbacher is the grape of Schilcher, the sharp rosé of western Styria; the name is usually traced to the German schillern, to shimmer, for its colour between pink and onion skin. Austrian Wine notes that only Blauer Wildbacher from Styria may bear the name. From the 2018 vintage the region became the Weststeiermark DAC, with three tiers of origin: the regional wine, the village wine and the single vineyard Riedenwein. Langmann bottles Schilcher from several Rieden, among them the Langegg, the Edla and the Hochgrail, a high slope of gneiss at about 550 metres, and makes it sparkling too. Three generations of the family work its steep vineyards. For a sommelier the Hochgrail shows Schilcher as a wine of place, not only a rosé for the tavern, and it teaches the grape, the colour and the acidity that make the Weststeiermark's own wine.

others.name: Schilcher Ried Langegg
others.note: From the home slope at Langegg, planted with the family's own selection of small, spicy berried Blauer Wildbacher.

others.name: Schilcher Ried Hochgrail Sonnenhang
others.note: From a sunnier, windier parcel of the Hochgrail, raised partly in small French oak.

others.name: Schilcher Brut Rosé Reserve
others.note: A sparkling Schilcher of the house.

traps: Schilcher is a rosé, never a red: Blauer Wildbacher is a dark grape, but the Weststeiermark DAC requires it to be made as rosé.
Lex is the farm's old house name, not a grape or a site: the wines are Langmann's, labelled Lex Langmann on some bottles.

cards.front: Langmann's Schilcher: which grape, and how must the Weststeiermark DAC have it made?
cards.back: Blauer Wildbacher alone, made as a rosé.

cards.front: By Langmann's own account, when did the family first plant vineyards at Langegg?
cards.back: In 1746, with Blauer Wildbacher and a field blend.

questions.q: A guest asks what rock gives Langmann's Schilcher Ried Hochgrail its salty edge. Which fits?
opts: Gneiss
Coral limestone
Volcanic basalt
Loess
questions.exp: The Hochgrail lies on lean brown earth over gneiss at about 550 metres; coral limestone is the rock of the Südsteiermark's Zieregg, not of the Weststeiermark.

questions.q: Where does the word Schilcher most likely come from?
opts: The German schillern, to shimmer
A village called Schilch near Stainz
The surname of a grower of Stainz
A Slovenian word meaning sour
questions.exp: The name is traced to schillern, to shimmer, for the wine's colour between pink and onion skin; no village or grower gave it its name in the sources read.

sources.title: Falstaff: Langmann 2020 Schilcher Weststeiermark DAC Reserve Ried Hochgrail

report: The plan's doubt over the wine is settled on the Ried Hochgrail: the house bottles Schilcher from the Langegg, the Edla and the Hochgrail, Falstaff lists the Hochgrail as a Weststeiermark DAC Reserve and a Riedenwein, and the house gives its site in detail; I propose a swap of the wine's name alone, from Schilcher to Schilcher Ried Hochgrail, the record already teaching it.
The record's name already holds the plan's word Schilcher, so it lints under the plan as it stands.
The founding year 1746 is the family's own claim, repeated by Steiermark's tourism pages, and is told as its account.
The cellar regime of the Hochgrail is not in the house's pages read, so the making says only what the DAC requires and what any Schilcher is: hand picked, made as a rosé, bottled dry and young.

Left out for want of a second source: the protection of the name Schilcher in Styrian law from 1976, the house's claim to be the first West Styrian estate with the Nachhaltig Austria seal, and the Hochgrail as the largest single Ried of the Weststeiermark.
The region record calls Langmann the Weststeiermark's Schilcher benchmark, a judgement the record does not repeat; the living members of the family are not named.
